newsitem.title: UK: SOCCER-WENGER GRAPPLES WITH ENGLISH FIXTURE CONUNDRUM.
newsitem.headline: SOCCER-WENGER GRAPPLES WITH ENGLISH FIXTURE CONUNDRUM.

text.p: His side had just coasted to victory while Manchester United had lost. But Arsenal manager Arsene Wenger still had an axe to grind last Saturday afternoon.

Not with his players, not with the opposition or the match officials, but with the seemingly haphazard fixture system in England which means Arsenal have played three matches more than some of their championship rivals.

When the dust settled on Monday night at the end of a messy extended weekend of soccer which boasted five different kick-off times in two competitions spread over three days, third-placed Arsenal had played 30 matches in the premier league.

Leaders United and second-placed Liverpool had played 29 games, as had Aston Villa. Newcastle, in fourth, and Sheffield Wednesday, in sixth, had played 28 matches while Wimbledon and Chelsea, both involved in the F.A. Cup on Sunday, had played 27.
It all makes the top of the table difficult to decipher and, according to Wenger, gives the teams with games in hand -- usually those involved in Cup runs -- an edge over their rivals.
"I can't see why a day can't be given over to Cup matches without having to play league matches as well," the Frenchman told a post-match news conference on Saturday.
"I would like to know the position of the other managers about that. I think everybody should play on the same weekend. If it is a Cup weekend then the teams that aren't in the Cup shouldn't play."
"I don't think its deliberate but I do think the fact some teams have played fewer matches than others gives them an advantage, however slight it may be."
Wenger seems to have a point.

When Wimbledon and Chelsea finally play their matches in hand the scramble for places in Europe next season will be that little bit closer to conclusion. The two sides will have a clearer idea of what they need to do, whether they must play to win or play to avoid defeat, than Arsenal had when they played their corresponding fixtures.
Games in hand appear to be a peculiarly English phenomenon.

In Italy all 18 serie A sides had played 23 matches each by the end of last weekend. In Spain all but two sides had played the same number of matches. The same was true of the top flights in Germany, France and the Netherlands.
A boom in television coverage is often put forward as a reason for the ever-increasing disruption to the schedule for English league matches, traditionally played at three p.m. on Saturdays.

But the Italians and the Spaniards also watch hours of live football on TV and, although kick-off times there are staggered to meet the demands of television, their leagues are organised in a way which ensures sides can keep abreast of one another in terms of number of games played.
So why is it so different in England?
One reason, as Wenger recognised, is the importance the English place on the F.A. Cup.

Cup matches are scheduled for weekends rather than -- as in Italy and Spain -- for the middle of the week, and when replays are needed they are often played at weekends too, meaning league matches have to be postponed.
Bringing the premier league into line with its continental counterparts would eliminate the distracting "ifs and buts" which result from games in hand and would make it fairer.
But, in an increasingly hectic schedule in which free weekends are fast becoming a thing of the past, it could also signal the end of F.A. Cup Saturdays.
Many English traditionalists would find that hard to accept.
